newsitem.title: KENYA: Reforms seen not healing Tanzania coffee industry.
newsitem.headline: Reforms seen not healing Tanzania coffee industry.

text.p: Reforms of the last three years have failed to heal Tanzania's ailing coffee industry, whose importance as a major foreign exchange earner has declined in recent years, coffee researchers said in a report on Tuesday.
Coffee experts A.K. Kashuliza and R.C. Tembele said despite acreage under coffee rising to 235,000 hectares now from 105,000 hectares 20 years ago, production had virtually stagnated.
Arabica yields had also continued to fall on low labour and fertiliser inputs and insufficient control of coffee berry disease, they said in the first major report on the sector.
The "Tanzania Coffee Marketing Study" said that taxes and levies levelled on coffee sales were too high and in some cases, the entire tax burden was then transferred to the growers.

"This is an area that requires urgent review by the government and relevant bodies to streamline taxes paid," the report said. "In some countries, such taxes have been scrapped to permit development of their coffee industry."
Jeremy LeFroy, of Africa Coffee Co, said, "Liberalisation is seen a convenient scapegoat for 25 years of neglect."

But LeFroy, who is chairman of the coffee traders' association, agreed taxes on the sector were too high, and added that Dar es Salaam port charges were much higher compared to Kenya or those applied to Ugandan coffee through the port.

"This limits ability of buyers paying higher prices to farmers -- these are matters about which we are not very hapopy at the moment," LeFroy told Reuters by telephone from the northern Tanzanian coffee town of Moshi.
The report said that participation of private traders in coffee marketing at the farm level had not resulted in the envisaged competitive prices.
It suggested issuing of single licences for each market player to operate in marketing at farm level, deal with processing, participate in auction and the export market.
It said that although private trade participation resulted in prompt cash payments, prices they paid were generally lower than those given by cooperative societies.

The report said that the businesses of old cooperative (smallholder) curing factories had gone down considerably after the licensing of private traders to do curing and noted that such factories had no future without outside financial help.

"The government and donors should join cooperative unions to raise equity finance to refurbish such factories. Joint ventures should also be sought to rehabilitate coffee estates which are currently producing minimal amounts," the report said.
The report called for specialised training in coffee spraying and other farming skills to improve production.

The report cited some of the problems leading to a decline in Tanzania's coffee grades as lack of incentive payment to farmers by cooperatives and private buyers and the participation of private buyers in the coffee market.

"The Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperatives report (1996) observes that whereas with market liberalisation it was expected that the entry of experienced exporters in the coffee buying would revive the interest in coffee quality, that has not happened," the report said.

The Tanzania Coffee Board has already projected a decline in production in 1996/97 to 41,000-43,000 tonnes from 53,000 tonnes in 1995/96. The report said quality was declining but LeFroy said there had been no single complaint on coffee quality this year. The report suggested reforms failed to reverse the trends.
Earnings from are seen slumping to $90 million in 1996/97 from $115 million in 1995/96 and $139 million in 1994/96.
